bio: Jerusalem, also called Zion, Jebus and Salem, was the chief city of ancient Israel in the hill country of Judah. It is the present-day city of Jerusalem, and the location shown here lies in its Old City. Its Canaanite king Adonizedek opposed Joshua (Josh 10:1). David made it his capital, reigning…

Egypt was the ancient kingdom of the Nile valley in the northeast corner of Africa. Its usual Hebrew name, Mizraim, is a dual form that Smith's Bible Dictionary links to the country's two parts, Upper Egypt (the valley) and Lower Egypt (the Delta). Abram went there during a famine (Gen 12:10).…

Babylon was the great city on the Euphrates that served as capital of the Babylonian (Chaldean) empire. Its ruins lie near Hillah in modern Iraq, about 50 miles south of Baghdad, which is where the location shown here is placed. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the name as the Greek form of Babel.…

Jordan is the main river of the land of Israel. It flows south from the foot of Mount Hermon, through Lake Huleh and the Sea of Galilee, to the Salt (Dead) Sea. It marked the eastern edge of Canaan, so "this side Jordan" and "beyond Jordan" were standard ways of dividing the land (Josh 15:5; 2 Kgs…

Moab was a country east of the Dead Sea and the Jordan, in present-day Jordan, bordered on the north by the Arnon (Num 22:36). Israel camped in the plains of Moab opposite Jericho before entering Canaan. There Balak king of Moab summoned Balaam, Moses delivered the law, and Israel mourned his death…

Zion was originally the fortified stronghold of the Jebusite city of Jerusalem, which David captured and renamed the city of David (2 Sam 5:7; 1 Chr 11:5). Solomon later brought the ark up from there to his new temple (1 Kgs 8:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary places this first Zion on the southeastern…

Assyria was a region on the upper Tigris River, probably in what is now northern Iraq, and the heart of a major Mesopotamian empire. Easton's Bible Dictionary derives the name from its early capital, Asshur on the Tigris. Genesis places the Tigris (Hiddekel) east of Assyria (Gen 2:14). Micah calls…

Samaria, meaning "watch-mountain" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was the capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel, and its name came to stand for the kingdom and its territory (1 Kgs 13:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that King Omri built the city on a hill bought from Shemer.…

Gilead was a hilly region east of the Jordan River, also called "mount Gilead" and "the land of Gilead." Jacob headed toward it after fleeing Laban (Gen 31:21), and traders carried balm and spices from it to Egypt (Gen 37:25; Jer 8:22). Its grazing land drew the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and Moses…

Edom was the region and nation south and southeast of the Dead Sea, also called the land of Seir, where Esau's descendants, the Edomites, settled (Gen 32:3; 36:43). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "red." Horite clans lived there earlier (Gen 36:21), and Edom had kings before Israel did (1…

Canaan, also called the Promised Land, was the region between the Jordan River and the Dead Sea on the east and the Mediterranean on the west. Terah's family set out from Ur for it (Gen 11:31), and Abraham lived there as a foreigner. Hebron, Shechem and Bethlehem lay within it (Gen 23:2; Gen 33:18;…

Syria is the King James name for the region north and northeast of Israel, called Aram in Hebrew. In the Old Testament it usually means the Aramean kingdom ruled from Damascus (1 Kgs 15:18). Its kings Benhadad, Hazael and Rezin repeatedly fought Israel and Judah, besieging Samaria and marching on…

Galilee was the northern region of the land of Israel; its Hebrew name means "circuit" or "district" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). In the Old Testament it lay in the hill country of Naphtali, where Kedesh was a city of refuge (Josh 20:7). Solomon gave Hiram of Tyre twenty of its cities, and the…

Bethel (of Palestine), meaning "house of God," was a town in the central hill country about 10 miles north of Jerusalem, west of Ai and south of Shiloh. Its earlier name was Luz (Gen 28:19). Abraham built an altar east of it on entering Canaan (Gen 12:8), and Jacob named the place and later…

Jericho was an ancient walled city on the plain west of the Jordan, north of the Dead Sea, called "the city of palm trees" (2 Chr 28:15). Israel camped in the plains of Moab opposite it before crossing the Jordan. Joshua sent spies there, and Rahab hid them. The city was shut up against Israel, its…

Hebron was an ancient city in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Kirjath-arba after Arba, a great man among the Anakim (Josh 14:15). It was said to have been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt (Num 13:22). Abram settled by Mamre at Hebron, and he buried Sarah in the cave of Machpelah…

Lebanon is the mountainous region north of Israel, named in Deuteronomy and Joshua as the northern limit of the land promised to Israel, reaching toward the Euphrates (Deut 1:7; Josh 1:4). Joshua 13:5 also mentions "Lebanon toward the sunrising," which Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries…

Damascus was an ancient city of Syria, about 130 miles northeast of Jerusalem, and the capital of the Aramean (Syrian) kingdom (Isa 7:8). It first appears in Abram's pursuit of the eastern kings and as the home of his steward Eliezer. David defeated the Syrians of Damascus and garrisoned the…

Bashan was a fertile region east of the Jordan River, north of Gilead, stretching toward Mount Hermon and east to Salcah. Before Israel arrived it was the kingdom of Og, an Amorite king who lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei. Israel defeated him in battle at Edrei. Moses then gave Bashan to the…

Tyre was a major Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, about 20 miles south of Sidon, at the modern town of Sur in Lebanon. It is first named as a "strong city" on Asher's border (Josh 19:29). Hiram king of Tyre sent cedar and craftsmen to build David's house and later supplied Solomon…

Sodom was a city of the plain near the Dead Sea. It is named with Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim at the edge of Canaanite territory (Gen 10:19). Lot settled near it after parting from Abram, and its men are described as exceedingly wicked (Gen 13:12–13). Its king fought in the vale of Siddim, where Lot…

Judea was the southern region of the land of Israel in New Testament times, lying west of the Jordan and south of Samaria, with Jerusalem as its chief city. The name derives from Judah, and Ezra 9:9 speaks of the restored community 'in Judah and in Jerusalem' after the exile. Bethlehem, where Jesus…

Midian was a desert region and people south and east of Canaan, named, according to Gen 25:2, after a son of Abraham by Keturah. Moses fled there from Pharaoh, served Jethro, the priest of Midian, and kept his flocks until God sent him back to Egypt. His sons Gershom and Eliezer were probably born…

Gibeah, meaning "a hill," was a town of Benjamin (Josh 18:28), also called Gibeah of Benjamin and Gibeah of Saul. In Judges a Levite stopped there for the night rather than lodge in a foreign city. The men of the town surrounded the house where he stayed and abused his concubine until she died.…

Shechem was a city in the hill country of central Canaan, later in the territory of Ephraim. Abram stopped there at the plain of Moreh on entering Canaan (Gen 12:6), about 1921 BC by inference from context. Jacob camped before the city on returning from Padan-aram, and his daughter was defiled…

Heshbon was the royal city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who had taken the land of the former king of Moab as far as the Arnon (Num 21:26). Israel captured it under Moses and settled in it and its villages (Num 21:25; Deut 2:24–30). The tribe of Reuben rebuilt it (Num 32:37), and it lay on the…

Negeb is the dry region in the far south of Canaan, south of the hill country of Judah. The name comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be dry." The King James Version usually translates it simply as "the south." Abram journeyed through it, and returned there from Egypt before going on to Bethel (Gen…

Gibeon was a large Hivite city, described as greater than Ai and one of the royal cities. Its people made peace with Joshua, and it was the only city that did so (Josh 11:19). When five Amorite kings attacked it for this, Joshua defeated them there, and in that battle he called on the sun to stand…

Gilgal was Israel's first camp west of the Jordan, on the east border of Jericho, where Joshua set up twelve stones taken from the river (Josh 4:19–20). The text links its name to the LORD "rolling away" the reproach of Egypt (Josh 5:9), and Israel kept the Passover there. It served as Joshua's…

Beersheba was a city in the far south of Israel. Genesis explains the name as "well of the oath", recalling the covenant Abraham and Abimelech swore there (Gen 21:31–32). A second account links the name to a well dug by Isaac's servants (Gen 26:33). Abraham planted a grove, worshipped and lived…

Bethlehem was a town in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Ephrath, on whose road Rachel was buried (Gen 35:19; 48:7). It was the home of the judge Ibzan and of Elimelech's family. Naomi returned there with Ruth, and Boaz lived there. David's family lived there too. Samuel came to the town…

Euphrates is the great river of western Asia, still known by that name, flowing from the mountains of eastern Turkey through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Genesis names it as the fourth river of Eden (Gen 2:14). Often called simply "the river" or "the great river," it marks the northeastern…

Gath was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, and one of the places where some of the Anakim remained after Joshua's conquest (Josh 11:22; 13:3). The Philistines carried the captured ark of God there (1 Sam 5:8). Gath was the home of the giant Goliath and of other men of great stature…

Ai was a Canaanite city east of Bethel, "beside Bethaven," whose name is usually taken to mean "the ruin" or "heap." Abraham camped and built an altar between Bethel and Ai (called Hai in the KJV) when he entered Canaan and again on his return from the south. Under Joshua, Israel's first small…

Mizpah (also spelled Mizpeh, meaning "watchtower") was a city of Benjamin near Jerusalem, one of several places with this name. The tribes of Israel assembled there before the LORD to act against Benjamin and swore oaths there (Judg 20:1; 21:1). Samuel gathered Israel there to fast and confess,…

The Nile is the great river of Egypt, flowing north through northeast Africa into the Mediterranean Sea. The King James Version never uses the name, and usually calls it simply "the river." Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat and seven lean cows coming up out of it (Gen 41:1–3, 17–18). He later ordered…

Shiloh was a city in the hill country of Ephraim where Israel set up the tabernacle after the conquest (Josh 18:1). There Joshua and Eleazar the priest divided the land among the tribes by lot (Josh 18:10; 19:51). The house of God stayed there through the time of the judges. It drew yearly pilgrims…

Sidon (also spelled Zidon) was an ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Tyre. It is the modern Saida in Lebanon, and the location shown here marks that site. Genesis names it as the northern limit of Canaanite territory. It lay within the area allotted to Asher, but Asher…

Nazareth was a town in Galilee, the home of Joseph and Mary, where the angel Gabriel announced Jesus' birth to Mary (Luke 1:26). Joseph left it for Bethlehem before the birth, and the family returned there afterward (Luke 2:4; Luke 2:39). Jesus was brought up there, and as an adult he read in its…

The Red Sea is the long arm of the Indian Ocean between Africa and Arabia. At its northern end it splits into the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba on either side of the Sinai Peninsula. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain its Hebrew name, Yam Suph, as "sea of weeds" or reeds. It is…

Persia was the empire, and originally the homeland, of the Persians, in what is now Iran. In the Bible it appears mainly as the power that followed Babylon. Babylon's captives served there "until the reign of the kingdom of Persia" (2 Chr 36:20), and Cyrus king of Persia proclaimed that the Jews…

Seir was a mountainous region, also called Mount Seir, identified with the country of Edom (Gen 32:3; Gen 36:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary places it along the eastern side of the Arabah, from the southeastern end of the Dead Sea toward the Gulf of Aqaba, in what is now southern Jordan. The location…

Gomorrah was a city of the plain of the Jordan, nearly always named alongside Sodom. Genesis lists it at the edge of Canaanite territory (Gen 10:19) and describes the region as well watered before its destruction (Gen 13:10). Its king, Birsha, joined the kings of Sodom, Admah, Zeboiim and Zoar in a…

Hamath was a major city of Syria, the capital of a kingdom of the same name, identified with modern Hama on the Orontes River; the location shown here follows that identification. Amos calls it "Hamath the great" (Amos 6:2). Its king Toi sent greetings to David after David defeated Hadadezer (2 Sam…

Carmel was a town in the hill country of Judah, listed with Maon, Ziph and Juttah (Josh 15:55). After his campaign against the Amalekites, Saul came there and set up a monument before moving on to Gilgal (1 Sam 15:12). The wealthy Nabal, who lived in nearby Maon, kept his flocks at Carmel and…

Jezreel was a town on the border of Issachar, named with Chesulloth and Shunem (Josh 19:18). It was part of the territory Abner placed under Ish-bosheth (2 Sam 2:9). King Ahab kept a palace there, and Naboth's vineyard lay next to it (1 Kgs 21:1). Elijah ran ahead of Ahab's chariot to its entrance…

Lachish was a fortified city in the lowlands (Shephelah) of southwestern Judah. Its Amorite king Japhia joined Adonizedek of Jerusalem's coalition against Gibeon. Joshua later took the city on the second day of the siege and defeated Horam of Gezer, who came to help it (Josh 10:3, 10:31–33). It was…

Gad was the territory east of the Jordan given to the tribe of Gad. Moses assigned it to them, along with Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh, from the conquered kingdoms of Sihon and Og (Num 32:33; Josh 13:8). Joshua 13:24–28 describes it as including Jazer, the cities of Gilead, and half the…

Macedonia was a Roman province north of Greece and the first part of Europe where Paul preached. In a night vision a man of Macedonia begged Paul, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us," and he crossed over to Philippi, described as the chief city of that part of the province (Acts 16:9–12). Paul…

Mount Zion was one of the hills on which Jerusalem stood, and its name is often used for the city itself, especially as the place where the LORD is said to dwell and reign (Ps 74:2; Isa 8:18; Mic 4:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it as the southeastern hill, the stronghold David took from…

Asher was the territory given to the tribe of Asher, named for Jacob's son, in the fifth lot of the land division (Josh 19:24). It ran along the Mediterranean coast from Mount Carmel northward toward Tyre and Sidon, with Manasseh to the south, Zebulun and Issachar to the southeast, and Naphtali to…

Dan was Israel's northernmost town, near the sources of the Jordan below Mount Hermon. Originally called Laish or Leshem, it was captured by members of the tribe of Dan, who renamed it after their ancestor (Josh 19:47; Judg 18:29). Its mention in Abram's pursuit of Lot's captors (Gen 14:14)…

Ekron was the northernmost of the five chief Philistine cities, each ruled by its own lord (Josh 13:3). It lay on Judah's northern border and was assigned first to Judah and then to Dan (Josh 15:11, 45–46; 19:43). Judah is said to have taken it (Judg 1:18), but it was later back in Philistine…

Mount Sinai, also called Horeb, is the mountain where the LORD came down in fire and smoke, the mountain quaked, and Moses was called to the summit (Exod 19:18–20). The people were kept back by boundaries set around it (Exod 19:23). There Moses received the two stone tablets, and later a second…

Ramoth-gilead was a fortified city east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead. Under Solomon it was the base of Ben-geber, an officer whose district included the towns of Jair and the region of Argob in Bashan (1 Kgs 4:13). Later the Syrians held it. Ahab of Israel, joined by Jehoshaphat of Judah,…

Susa, called Shushan in the King James Version, was a royal city in the province of Elam, where the Persian king kept a palace or citadel. Daniel saw a vision there beside the river Ulai (Dan 8:2), and Nehemiah was serving there when he heard news of Jerusalem (Neh 1:1). Most of the events of the…

Ashdod was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, near the Mediterranean coast between Gaza and Joppa. Some of the Anakim still lived there after Joshua's conquest. It was allotted to Judah, though it was listed among the lands still remaining to be taken (Josh 13:3; 15:47). After…

Gaza, called Azzah in some passages (1 Kgs 4:24; Jer 25:20), was a city near the Mediterranean coast in the far southwest of Canaan, on the route toward Egypt. Gen 10:19 names it as a limit of Canaanite territory. Joshua's campaigns reached it, and some Anakim remained there. It was allotted to…

West Manasseh was the territory of the half of the tribe of Manasseh that settled west of the Jordan River, in the central hill country of Canaan. The other half held Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan (Josh 17:1, 17:5–6). The western lot went to the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem,…

Amalek is the name of a nomadic people and of the desert region they roamed south of Canaan. Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim soon after the exodus. Joshua defeated them while Moses held up his hand on a hill, and the LORD declared war with Amalek "from generation to generation." Deuteronomy…

Asia in the New Testament is the Roman province covering western Asia Minor, in present-day western Turkey, with Ephesus as its capital (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Jews from Asia were in Jerusalem at Pentecost and later disputed with Stephen (Acts 2:9; 6:9). On his second…

Nineveh was a great city on the east bank of the Tigris and the capital of the Assyrian empire. Gen 10:11 says Asshur built it, or, in the Revised Version's reading, Nimrod. This entry follows the Nimrod reading. Sennacherib king of Assyria returned to live there after his campaign against Judah (2…

Sinai is the desert region, and the mountain within it, where the Israelites camped after leaving Egypt. They came from Rephidim into the wilderness of Sinai in the third month after the Exodus and camped before the mount (Exod 19:1–2). While they were there, Moses received commands about the…

Beth-shemesh, meaning "house of the sun" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a city on the northern border of Judah, near the Philistine lowland (Josh 15:10). It was given with its pasturelands to the Levites (Josh 21:16; 1 Chr 6:59). When the Philistines sent back the ark of the LORD on a cart, the…

Ephesus was a major city of the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of Asia Minor. Its ruins lie near modern Selçuk in Turkey. The city was known as the guardian of the goddess Diana's worship (Acts 19:35). Paul first stopped there briefly, reasoning in the synagogue before sailing for…

Ramah was a city in the territory of Benjamin, listed with Gibeon and Beeroth (Josh 18:25). It lay near Gibeah on the road north from Jerusalem, and Deborah judged Israel between Ramah and Bethel (Judg 4:5; 19:13). Baasha king of Israel fortified it to blockade Asa king of Judah. He later abandoned…

Caesarea was a port city on the Mediterranean coast of Judea, about 70 miles northwest of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Herod the Great built it on the site of an older town called Strato's Tower and named it after Caesar Augustus. It became the seat of the Roman governors. In Acts,…

Capernaum was a city of Galilee on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, mentioned only in the Gospels. After leaving Nazareth, Jesus settled there, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matt 4:13), and it became a main center of his ministry. He taught in its synagogue on the sabbath (Mark 1:21; Luke…

Cush was a region south of Egypt, usually rendered "Ethiopia" in the King James Version. Ezekiel describes Egypt as stretching "from the tower of Syene" (probably modern Aswan) to the border of Cush (Ezek 29:10), and the prophets regularly pair it with Egypt (Isa 20:3–5; Ezek 30:4; Nah 3:9). Its…

Horeb is the mountain called "the mountain of God," where Moses came while tending Jethro's flock (Exod 3:1) and where the Israelites camped during the Wilderness Wanderings. There God made a covenant with Israel, spoke to the people out of the fire, and gave the law that Moses placed in the ark as…

Naphtali was the territory in northern Israel allotted to the tribe of Naphtali, which received the sixth lot when the land was divided (Josh 19:32–39). Its border ran along the Jordan on the east, with Zebulun to the south and Asher to the west. It contained nineteen fortified cities, including…

River, in the phrase "beyond the river" (also rendered "on this side the river" in the King James Version), was the Persian name for the region west of the river, which is by inference the Euphrates. Seen from the Persian court, this territory, including Samaria and Judah, lay "beyond" it. The…

Zebulun was the territory allotted to the Israelite tribe descended from Jacob's son Zebulun. It lay in what was later called lower Galilee, and the location shown here is in the hills near Nazareth. Jacob's blessing links Zebulun with the sea and with ships, reaching toward Sidon (Gen 49:13). In…

Anathoth was a town in the territory of Benjamin that was given, with its pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron (Josh 21:18; 1 Chr 6:60). Solomon banished the priest Abiathar to his fields there (1 Kgs 2:26). Abiezer, one of David's monthly army commanders, came from Anathoth (1 Chr…

Arabah is the Hebrew name for the deep rift valley that runs from the Sea of Galilee down the Jordan valley to the Dead Sea and on south to the Gulf of Aqaba. The King James Version usually translates it "the plain" and keeps "Arabah" only in Josh 18:18, which describes Benjamin's border. It is…

Ephraim (Territory) was the land allotted to the tribe of Ephraim, descended from Joseph's son Ephraim, in the central hill country west of the Jordan. Joshua 16 traces its borders. The south ran from the Jordan near Jericho up past Bethel, then west by lower Beth-horon and Gezer to the…

Kadesh, also called Kadesh-Barnea, was an oasis in the wilderness of Zin, on the southern edge of Canaan near the border of Edom. In Abraham's time it was also called En-mishpat, and it served as a landmark for his travels and for the well where Hagar met the angel. Kadesh was Israel's main camp in…

Keilah was a walled town in the lowlands of Judah, listed among the cities of Judah's territory with Achzib and Mareshah (Josh 15:44). When Philistines raided its threshing floors, David, after twice asking the LORD, went down with his men, defeated them and rescued the town (1 Sam 23:1–5). The…

Kiriath-jearim was a city in the hill country west of Jerusalem. It was one of the four Gibeonite cities that Israel reached in Josh 9:17. It was also called Baalah and Kiriath-baal, and it stood on the boundary between Judah and Benjamin, where it is assigned to Judah. The "Kirjath" listed among…

Libnah was a Canaanite royal city in the Shephelah (lowland) of Judah, near Lachish. Joshua captured it after Makkedah, killed its king and then moved on to Lachish (Josh 10:29–32, 39; 12:15). It was later assigned to Judah and given, with its pasturelands, to the priestly descendants of Aaron…

Antioch (Syria) was a major city on the Orontes River, capital of the Roman province of Syria and, according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, the third city of the Roman empire after Rome and Alexandria. It is the modern Antakya in southern Turkey. Believers scattered by the persecution after…

Benjamin (Territory) was the land allotted by lot to the tribe of Benjamin, lying between Judah to the south and the descendants of Joseph to the north (Josh 18:11). Its northern border ran from the Jordan past Jericho and up through the hill country toward Bethel (Luz). It then descended past…

East Manasseh (Half-Tribe) was the territory east of the Jordan River settled by half of the tribe of Manasseh. It covered northern Gilead and the former kingdom of Og in Bashan. Moses assigned it after the clans of Machir, Manasseh's son, captured Gilead from the Amorites. Jair took the towns he…

Elam was an ancient country east of Babylonia. The location shown here is in the lowlands and hills of what is now southwestern Iran, around the modern province of Khuzestan. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name as an Assyrian word meaning "high" and links the people to Elam, a son of Shem…

Geba, whose name means "hill," was a town in the territory of Benjamin, also spelled Gaba (Josh 18:24). It was given to the Levites (Josh 21:17; 1 Chr 6:60). In Saul's early reign the Philistines kept a garrison there until Jonathan attacked it (1 Sam 13:3). King Asa fortified Geba with stones and…

Gezer was an ancient Canaanite royal city in the foothills west of Jerusalem, between lower Beth-horon and the Mediterranean (Josh 16:3). Its king Horam came to help Lachish and was destroyed by Joshua (Josh 10:33). It marked the western edge of Ephraim's territory and was given with its…

The Holy Place was the outer room of Israel's sanctuary, lying in front of the inner sanctuary, called the "oracle" or Most Holy Place. Heb 9:2 describes the tabernacle's first room as holding the lampstand, the table and the showbread. In Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, the ends of the ark's…

Joppa was an ancient seaport on the Mediterranean coast, listed on the border of Dan's territory (called Japho in Josh 19:46). It served as the landing point for cedar from Lebanon, floated down the coast for Solomon's temple and again for the rebuilding of the temple after the exile, then carried…

The Mount of Olives, also called mount Olivet, is the ridge east of Jerusalem, facing the temple across the Kidron Valley. David climbed it weeping and barefoot as he fled from Absalom (2 Sam 15:30). Zechariah foretold that the Lord's feet would stand on it and that it would split from east to…

Rabbah, also called Rabbath of the children of Ammon, was the chief city of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan. Deut 3:11 says the giant iron bedstead of Og, king of Bashan, was kept there. It lay beyond the land given to Gad (Josh 13:25). David sent Joab to besiege it, and David stayed in Jerusalem…

Issachar was the region allotted to the tribe of Issachar, named after Jacob's son (Gen 30:18). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as 'reward.' It was the fourth lot drawn when Joshua divided the land. Its border ran by Jezreel, Chesulloth and Shunem, reached Tabor, and ended at…

Mahanaim was a town east of the Jordan River, near the Jabbok. Its name means "two camps". Jacob gave it the name after meeting God's angels there on his way home (Gen 32:2). It marked a boundary between the lands of Gad and eastern Manasseh (Josh 13:26, 30). It was also given with its pasturelands…

Ramah was the hometown of Elkanah and Hannah and the home of their son Samuel, the city of Mount Ephraim called Ramathaim-zophim in 1 Sam 1:1. Samuel lived there as judge of Israel and built an altar there. The elders came to him at Ramah to ask for a king, and he returned there after anointing…

Tirzah was a city in the hill country of central Israel. Its king appears among the Canaanite rulers defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:24). It later served as a royal residence and capital of the northern kingdom. Jeroboam's household lived there (1 Kgs 14:17), and Baasha, Elah, Zimri and Omri reigned…

Ammon was the land of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan River and north of Moab, near the upper Jabbok River. On the way from Egypt, Israel was told not to take it, because it had been given to the descendants of Lot (Deut 2:19, 37). Easton's Bible Dictionary traces the people to Ammon, or…

Arnon was the river, flowing through a deep valley east of the Dead Sea, that formed the border between Moab to the south and the Amorites to the north (Num 21:13; Judg 11:18). On their way to Canaan the Israelites went around Moab and camped beyond the Arnon. They then defeated Sihon, king of the…

Cyprus is a large island in the eastern Mediterranean, about 60 miles off the Syrian coast, and still known by that name today. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify it with the Old Testament "Chittim" (Kittim), which the prophets mention as a place…

Great Sea is the biblical name for the Mediterranean Sea, which formed the western border of the land promised to Israel. Numbers sets it as the west boundary, and the northern boundary line also starts from it (Num 34:6–7). Joshua uses it to describe the western limit of the land, toward the…

Jabesh-gilead was a city in Gilead, east of the Jordan River. When it sent no one to the assembly at Mizpah against Benjamin, Israel's forces killed its inhabitants and spared 400 young women, who were given as wives to the surviving Benjamites (Judg 21:8–14). Later Nahash the Ammonite besieged it,…

Jazer (also spelled Jaazer) was an Amorite city east of the Jordan. Moses sent men to spy it out, and Israel took its surrounding villages and drove out the Amorites (Num 21:32). Its land was good for cattle, and the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked for it. Gad rebuilt it (Num 32:1, 35), and it…

Megiddo was a Canaanite royal city on the southern edge of the Jezreel Valley, whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:21). It was assigned to Manasseh, but the tribe did not drive out its Canaanite inhabitants (Josh 17:11; Judg 1:27). Deborah's song places the battle against the kings of Canaan 'by…

The Most Holy Place was the innermost room of the temple, where the ark of the covenant was kept. In Solomon's temple it was an inner chamber, also called the oracle, lined with cedar, twenty cubits square, overlaid with fine gold and closed by gold doors (1 Kgs 6:16; 2 Chr 3:8; 1 Kgs 7:50). Two…

Reuben was the territory given to the tribe of Reuben, descendants of Jacob's eldest son, east of the Jordan River in what is now central Jordan. Moses assigned it to the tribe by families (Josh 13:15). It ran north from Aroer on the Arnon River (probably the modern Wadi Mujib) across the plain…

Ziklag was a town in the Negev, the southern region of Judah. It is listed among Judah's towns (Josh 15:31) and among those given to Simeon (Josh 19:5; 1 Chr 4:30). Later it was held by the Philistines, and Achish, king of Gath, gave it to David, after which it belonged to the kings of Judah (1 Sam…

Ashkelon was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, a seaport on the Mediterranean coast north of Gaza. Its location is not in doubt: it is the ancient site of Ashkelon in modern Israel, near the present-day city of the same name, and the location shown here matches that site. Judah is…

Bethany was a village at the Mount of Olives, about fifteen furlongs (roughly 2 miles) from Jerusalem (John 11:18). It was the home of Lazarus and his sisters Mary and Martha (John 11:1), and the place where Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead. In his last week Jesus lodged at Bethany and went into…

Goshen was a region of Egypt where Jacob and his family settled during the time of Joseph, and where the Israelites lived until the Exodus. Joseph offered it to his family so they could live near him with their flocks and herds (Gen 45:10). Joseph met Jacob there (Gen 46:28–29), and Pharaoh granted…

Hazor was a major Canaanite city in northern Israel, described as formerly "the head of all those kingdoms" (Josh 11:10). Its king Jabin gathered a northern coalition against Joshua, who captured Hazor, killed its people and burned it, the only city of that region he burned (Josh 11:1, 11:13). It…

Riblah was a city "in the land of Hamath" in Syria that foreign kings used as a military headquarters during campaigns against Judah. Pharaoh Necho held King Jehoahaz in chains there and imposed tribute on Judah (2 Kgs 23:33). Later Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon based himself at Riblah during the siege…

River of Arnon is the stream and deep gorge east of the Dead Sea that marked the southern limit of Israel's land beyond the Jordan. Modern versions such as the ESV call it the Valley of the Arnon, because the Hebrew word can mean either a seasonal stream or the ravine it runs through. Israel…

Zobah was an Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Israel in the time of Saul, David and Solomon. Saul fought "the kings of Zobah" (1 Sam 14:47), suggesting it then had several rulers. Under David it was ruled by Hadadezer son of Rehob, whom David defeated as Hadadezer went to secure his border at the…

Achaia was the Roman province covering southern Greece, including the Peloponnesus, with Corinth as its main city. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name once meant a narrow strip on the northern Peloponnesus, but the New Testament always uses it for the larger province. It was governed by a…

Haran was a city in Upper Mesopotamia where Terah settled with Abram, Sarai and Lot after leaving Ur of the Chaldees on the way to Canaan, and where Terah died (Gen 11:31–32). Abram left Haran for Canaan at seventy-five, taking his household and the possessions gathered there (Gen 12:4–5). By…

Kadesh-barnea was a desert oasis on the southern edge of the promised land, an eleven days' journey from Horeb by way of Mount Seir (Deut 1:2). After leaving Horeb, Israel crossed the wilderness and arrived here (Deut 1:19). From Kadesh-barnea Moses sent spies, including Caleb, to explore Canaan.…

Lebo-hamath was a place on the far northern edge of the land promised to Israel. The King James Version translates the Hebrew as "the entering in of Hamath," treating it as the approach to the Syrian city of Hamath. Many modern translations read it as a town name, Lebo-hamath. It marks the northern…

Mount Hor was a mountain on the border of Edom where the Israelites camped after leaving Kadesh during their wilderness journey. Here God told Moses to take Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain in full view of the people, and Aaron died there at 123 years old, in the fortieth year after the…

Mount Seir was the mountain range given to Esau's descendants, the Edomites, as their homeland (Deut 2:5). It lay on the route from Horeb to Kadesh-barnea (Deut 1:2), and the Israelites travelled around it for many days during their wilderness journey (Deut 2:1). God forbade Israel to take any of…

Paddan-aram was the region in northern Mesopotamia where Abraham's relatives lived, in Genesis. It was the home of Bethuel and his son Laban, whose sister Rebekah became Isaac's wife (Gen 25:20). Isaac later sent Jacob there to find a wife among Laban's daughters rather than among the Canaanites…

River, often "the River" in the Hebrew Bible, refers in these passages to the Euphrates, the great river of Mesopotamia. Deut 11:24 names it outright as the northeastern limit of the land promised to Israel. Balaam's hometown of Pethor lay "by the river" (Num 22:5), probably on the Euphrates. In…

Succoth, meaning "booths", was a city east of the Jordan, in the valley near the Jabbok River. Jacob settled there after parting from Esau. He built a house and made booths for his cattle, which gave the place its name (Gen 33:17). It later fell to the tribe of Gad as part of the former kingdom of…

Aijalon was a town in the low hills northwest of Jerusalem, allotted to the tribe of Dan and given to the Kohathite Levites (Josh 19:42; Josh 21:24; 1 Chr 6:69). The valley of the same name is where Joshua called on the moon to stand still (Josh 10:12). Amorites held on there, though the house of…

Aroer was a city on the northern edge of the Arnon gorge, east of the Dead Sea. It marked the southern limit of the kingdom of Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon (Josh 12:2). After Israel took his land, Moses gave the region running north from Aroer to the tribes of Reuben and Gad (Deut 2:36; Deut…

Chaldea was the region of southern Mesopotamia around Babylon, the alluvial plain formed by the Euphrates and Tigris near the Persian Gulf. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Chaldea proper as the southern part of Babylonia, though the name was commonly used for the whole Mesopotamian plain.…

Dan was the region allotted to the tribe of Dan, the seventh lot drawn when Joshua divided the land west of the Jordan. It lay between Judah and Ephraim and stretched toward the Mediterranean coast. Its towns included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Aijalon, Timnah, Ekron, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Jehud and…

Debir was a Canaanite town in the hill country of Judah, earlier called Kirjath-sepher (Josh 15:15; Judg 1:11) and also Kirjath-sannah (Josh 15:49). Joshua captured it, killed its king and destroyed its inhabitants (Josh 10:38–39), and its king appears in the list of defeated kings (Josh 12:13). It…

Dibon was a city east of the Jordan, north of the Arnon River, that changed hands between Moab and Israel. An old victory song over Moab mentions it (Num 21:30), which suggests it was originally Moabite. The Gadites and Reubenites named it among the lands they asked Moses for (Num 32:3), and Gad is…

Gerar was an ancient city in the far south of Canaan, near Gaza, named as a point on the Canaanite border (Gen 10:19). Abraham lived there for a time, and its king, Abimelech, took Sarah after Abraham said she was his sister (Gen 20:1–2). During a later famine Isaac also settled in Gerar, where the…

Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom east of the Jordan, called "Geshur in Syria" (2 Sam 15:8). The Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites, who went on living among them (Josh 13:13). In David's time its king was Talmai son of Ammihud. His daughter Maacah married David and was the mother of…

Hormah was a Canaanite town in the far south of Canaan, earlier called Zephath (Judg 1:17). Its name is usually explained as meaning "devoted to destruction" or "banned" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Israelites who tried to enter the land against Moses' warning were driven back as far as Hormah by…

Kedar was the land and people of a nomadic Arab tribe in the deserts east of Israel, named after Ishmael's second son (Gen 25:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary places them in northwestern Arabia, and the rough location shown here lies in that region. The biblical writers knew Kedar for its tents, used…

Kedesh, also called Kedesh in Galilee, was a city in the hill country of Naphtali in northern Israel. It was originally a Canaanite royal city whose king Joshua defeated (Josh 12:22). It was allotted to Naphtali and later set apart as a city of refuge for someone who had killed another person. It…

Kidron was a seasonal torrent valley just outside Jerusalem, on its eastern side between the city and the Mount of Olives, according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. David crossed it weeping as he fled from Absalom toward the wilderness (2 Sam 15:23), and Solomon made crossing it the…

Michmash was a town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, set on the north side of a steep gorge facing Gibeah and Geba to the south. Saul first held it with two thousand men (1 Sam 13:2). The Philistines then camped there in force (1 Sam 13:5, 16), and their garrison guarded the "passage of Michmash,"…

Rome was the capital of the Roman Empire, in Italy, and is the modern city of the same name. Visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, were in Jerusalem at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). The emperor Claudius once expelled all Jews from the city, which brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth (Acts…

Salt Sea is the biblical name for the lake now called the Dead Sea, at the southern end of the Jordan valley. It is also called "the sea of the plain" (Deut 3:17; Josh 3:16; Josh 12:3). Gen 14:3 says the vale of Siddim, where the kings gathered for battle in Abraham's day, "is the salt sea," which…

Zoar was a small city in the plain of the Jordan, earlier called Bela (Gen 14:2, 8). Its king joined the kings of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim in battle in the vale of Siddim. When Sodom was destroyed, Lot fled to Zoar, and Genesis ties the name, meaning "little," to that episode (Gen…

Zorah was a town in the low hill country (the Shephelah) west of Jerusalem. It appears among the towns of Judah under the spelling Zoreah (Josh 15:33) and is later listed in the inheritance of Dan, alongside Eshtaol (Josh 19:41). It was the home of Manoah, Samson's father (Judg 13:2). The Spirit of…

Adullam was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, listed with Jarmuth, Socoh and Azekah. It was once the seat of a Canaanite king defeated by Joshua, and Gen 38:1 already mentions it in the story of Judah. Rehoboam later fortified it, and Jews resettled it after the return from Babylon. Micah…

Chebar was a river or waterway in "the land of the Chaldeans" (Babylonia), where some of the Jews taken captive from Judah lived. The priest Ezekiel was among these exiles when he saw his first visions of God beside it (Ezek 1:1–3). Exiles also lived there at Tel-abib (Ezek 3:15). Ezekiel later…

Cilicia was a Roman province on the southeastern coast of Asia Minor, between the Taurus Mountains and the Mediterranean, in what is now southern Turkey around Adana. Its chief city, Tarsus, was Paul's birthplace (Acts 21:39; 22:3), and the governor Felix noted that Paul came from this province…

Edrei was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan, and one of the two royal cities of Og, king of Bashan, the other being Ashtaroth. Og came out with his whole army to fight the Israelites under Moses at Edrei and was defeated, and his kingdom passed to Israel. Edrei marked a limit of Og's realm, with…

Eglon was a Canaanite royal city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah, near Lachish. Its king, Debir, joined the alliance of five Amorite kings led by Adonizedek of Jerusalem that attacked Gibeon (Josh 10:3–5). After the coalition's defeat, the five kings were brought out of a cave and put to death…

The Brook of Egypt (the "river of Egypt" in the King James Version) was a seasonal watercourse at the southwestern edge of Israel's land, between Canaan and Egypt. It marked the end of Israel's promised southern border, which ran from Azmon to the Mediterranean (Num 34:5; Josh 15:4), and it bounded…

Jabesh is a shortened form of Jabesh-gilead, a town east of the Jordan in Gilead, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "dryness." When Nahash the Ammonite besieged it, its men offered to submit to him. The elders asked for seven days to seek help from…

Jezreel is the name of a city, one of several places in the Bible called Jezreel. Josh 15:56 lists a Jezreel among the towns of the hill country of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary places it southeast of Hebron, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unidentified. Ahinoam "the…

The Kingdom of Judah was the southern Israelite kingdom that formed when the united monarchy split after Solomon's death. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, kept rule over the Israelites living in Judah's cities, and he gathered the men of Judah and Benjamin in an attempt to win back the northern tribes (1…

Makkedah was a Canaanite royal city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. After Joshua defeated the five allied Amorite kings at Gibeon, Israel pursued their forces as far as Azekah and Makkedah. The five kings hid in a cave there, and when this was reported, Joshua had them shut inside until the…

Media was an ancient country in what is now western and northwestern Iran, the homeland of the Medes. In the books of Esther and Daniel it is closely joined with Persia. The Persian king's court included the "seven princes of Persia and Media" (Esth 1:14), royal acts were recorded in "the…

Memphis was the ancient capital of Lower (northern) Egypt, on the west bank of the Nile about 12 miles south of modern Cairo. The location shown here matches the ruins near the village of Mit Rahina. In the King James Bible it appears as Memphis only in Hos 9:6, where the Hebrew is Moph. Elsewhere…

Paran was a desert region south of Canaan, usually called "the wilderness of Paran." Ishmael lived there after leaving Abraham's household, and his mother found him a wife from Egypt (Gen 21:21). After leaving Sinai, the Israelites' guiding cloud stopped there, and they camped there after Hazeroth…

Shinar was the early Hebrew name for the lowland plain of southern Mesopotamia between the lower Tigris and Euphrates, later known as Babylonia. Genesis names it as the land where Nimrod's kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh, about 1822 BC by inference from context (Gen 10:10). It was…

Timnah was a town on the northern border of Judah's territory, near Beth-shemesh (Josh 15:10). Judah went up to Timnah (spelled Timnath in the King James Version) to shear his sheep, and Tamar waited for him by the road leading there (Gen 38:12–14). In Samson's day it was a Philistine town with…

Topheth (also spelled Tophet) was a site in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem, where people burned their sons and daughters in fire as offerings to Molech (Jer 7:31). King Josiah defiled it as part of his religious reforms so that the practice would stop (2 Kgs 23:10). Jeremiah was sent…

The Valley of Rephaim was a valley just southwest of Jerusalem, on the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. The boundary descriptions in Josh 15:8 and Josh 18:16, where the King James Version calls it "the valley of the giants," place it at the north end near the valley of Hinnom, and…

n: Valley of the Son of Hinnom
bio: The Valley of the Son of Hinnom was a valley beside Jerusalem, also called the valley of the children of Hinnom. It contained Topheth, a site of high places where people burned their sons and daughters in fire as offerings to Molech and Baal (Jer 7:31; 32:35). By inference from the surrounding…

Azekah was a fortified town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah, listed among Judah's towns next to Socoh (Josh 15:35). Joshua's forces pursued the defeated Amorite kings from Gibeon as far as Azekah, and hailstones fell on the fleeing army along that route (Josh 10:10–11). Before David…

Beth-aven, whose name means "house of nothingness" or "house of wickedness," was a place in the hill country of Benjamin, east of Bethel and near Ai (Josh 7:2). Its wilderness marked part of Benjamin's northern border (Josh 18:12). In Saul's time the Philistines camped at Michmash, east of…

Beth-horon was a town in the hill country northwest of Jerusalem, on the route down from Gibeon toward the western lowlands. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe it as two villages, an upper and a lower Beth-horon, about 2 miles apart, linked by a steep ascent; Easton's explains the…

Bethsaida was a town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee. It was the hometown of Philip and also of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44), and John 12:21 calls it "Bethsaida of Galilee." Jesus fed the five thousand in a remote place belonging to the town (Luke 9:10). He sent his disciples across the…

Bozrah was a leading city of Edom, home of Zerah, whose son Jobab became one of the early kings of Edom before Israel had kings (Gen 36:33; 1 Chr 1:44). The prophets name it as a stronghold of Edom that would face judgment. Isaiah describes a great slaughter there, and also pictures a figure coming…

Eshtaol was a town in the lowland (the Shephelah), listed among the cities of Judah (Josh 15:33) and also counted within the inheritance of the tribe of Dan (Josh 19:41). It is almost always named together with neighboring Zorah. Between the two towns lay the "camp of Dan," where the Spirit of the…

Ezion-geber was a city and harbour on the Gulf of Aqaba, the northeastern arm of the Red Sea, always named beside Elath (Eloth) in Edomite territory. During the wilderness journey Israel camped there before moving on to Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, and later passed by it on the way toward Moab.…

Hermon is a high mountain at the northern edge of the land east of the Jordan, marking the far limit of the territory Israel took from the Amorites, which ran from Aroer on the Arnon to Hermon (Deut 4:48). The Sidonians called it Sirion and the Amorites Shenir (Deut 3:9), and it is also called Sion…

The Jabbok is a river east of the Jordan, which it joins roughly midway between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea. It is generally identified with the modern Zarqa River (Nahr ez-Zerqa, "blue river") in Jordan. Jacob crossed its ford by night with his wives, servants and eleven sons on his way…

Kiriath-arba was the earlier name of Hebron, a town in the hill country of Judah. The name means "city of Arba," and Josh 14:15 explains that Arba was a great man among the Anakim. Sarah died there, and Abraham mourned her (Gen 23:2). Jacob later came there to his father Isaac at Mamre, where…

Mesopotamia, meaning "between the rivers," is the Greek name for the land between the Euphrates and Tigris, largely in modern Iraq. In the Old Testament it translates the Hebrew Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers," which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean chiefly the northwestern part, near…

Mount Hermon is a prominent mountain marking the northern limit of the land Israel took east of the Jordan, which stretched "from the river Arnon unto mount Hermon" (Deut 3:8; Josh 12:1). Og, king of Bashan, ruled in Mount Hermon (Josh 12:5), and Baalgad "under mount Hermon" marked the northern…

Nebo was a town east of the Jordan, on the plateau north of the Dead Sea, distinct from Mount Nebo and from the Nebo in Judah, though it probably took its name from the nearby mountain. It is listed among the towns of the former Amorite territory that the tribes of Reuben and Gad asked Moses for.…

Taanach was a Canaanite royal city on the southwestern edge of the plain of Esdraelon (Jezreel), almost always named alongside nearby Megiddo. Its king was among those defeated by Joshua (Josh 12:21). Although it lay within Issachar's territory, it was counted to Manasseh (Josh 17:11; 1 Chr 7:29),…

Tekoa was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Bethlehem on the edge of the wilderness that runs down toward the Dead Sea. Joab brought a wise woman from Tekoa to persuade David, through a staged plea, to allow Absalom to return (2 Sam 14:2–9). Rehoboam fortified it along with Bethlehem…

Zin was a desert region on the southern edge of Canaan, usually called the wilderness of Zin. Kadesh lay within it (Num 20:1; 33:36), and the Israelites camped there during their wanderings. Miriam died and was buried at Kadesh in Zin. It was also where the dispute at the waters of Meribah took…

Zoan was an ancient city in the eastern Nile Delta of Egypt, known to the Greeks as Tanis and probably the modern village of San el-Hagar. The location shown here follows that identification. Num 13:22 notes that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan. The Psalms set God's wonders in Egypt in…

Ar, also called Ar of Moab, was a leading city or district of Moab on the border near the Arnon valley. During Israel's wilderness journey, God told Moses not to fight the Moabites, because Ar had been given to Lot's descendants (Deut 2:9). Israel passed through the region of Ar, and the Moabites…

Arabia was the broad desert region south and east of Israel, roughly the Arabian Peninsula and the Syrian desert to its north. In the Old Testament it is tied to kings and nomadic peoples. The kings of Arabia brought gold and silver to Solomon (2 Chr 9:14). Isaiah addresses an oracle to Arabia that…

Aroer was a city east of the Jordan built by the tribe of Gad (Num 32:34). Joshua 13:25 describes it as "before Rabbah," the Ammonite capital, marking the edge of Gad's territory toward Ammon. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be the Aroer from which Jephthah struck the Ammonites as far as…

Arpad was a city in northern Syria, always mentioned in the Bible alongside Hamath. Its name also appears as Arphad. In the Rabshakeh's speech to Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day, the Assyrians cited Arpad, its gods and its king as examples of peoples who could not withstand Assyria (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13;…

Ashtaroth was a city of Bashan, east of the Jordan, where Og king of Bashan lived and ruled alongside Edrei (Deut 1:4; Josh 12:4; Josh 13:12). Israel's defeat of Og under Moses was remembered as a well-known victory, and the Gibeonites mentioned it when they sought a treaty with Joshua (Josh 9:10).…

Babylonia was the region of southern Mesopotamia, the alluvial plain watered by the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, with Babylon as its chief city. It lies in what is now central and southern Iraq. In the verses shown here, the King James text says simply "Babylon," but the sense is the wider land…

Bahurim was a village east of Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin, on the road down toward the Jordan valley. Here Abner sent back Michal's husband, who had followed her weeping as she was returned to David (2 Sam 3:16). When David fled from Absalom, Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite of Bahurim…

Beeroth, whose name means "wells," was a city north of Jerusalem. It was one of four cities, with Gibeon, Chephirah and Kirjath-jearim, whose people made a peace treaty with Joshua after Israel's arrival. The wider passage identifies them as Hivites who won the treaty by deception (Josh 9:17). The…

Corinth was a Greek city on the isthmus joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece, about 48 miles west of Athens according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. The location shown here is the site of ancient Corinth, near the modern town. Its harbors made it a major trading center, and the city of Paul's…

Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa, west of Egypt, in the region Acts 2:10 calls the parts of Libya around Cyrene. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Greek colonists founded it about 630 BC and that it later had a large Jewish population. Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus, was…

Dedan was an Arabian people and region known for trade, according to the STEPBible Proper Names. Ezekiel lists the men of Dedan among the merchants of Tyre, bringing ivory tusks and ebony and trading in saddlecloths for riding (Ezek 27:15, 20). It is also paired with Sheba as a trading people (Ezek…

East, in the phrases "the children of the east" and "the men of the east," refers to the peoples of the desert lands east of Israel rather than to a single town. In Judges they joined the Midianites and Amalekites in raiding Israel after the crops were sown. They gathered in the valley of Jezreel…

Engedi was a town in the wilderness of Judah on the western shore of the Dead Sea, listed among Judah's cities in Josh 15:62. Its name means "fountain of the kid" (Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries), and it is identified with the spring and oasis of modern Ein Gedi (Ain Jidy), which the…

Galatia was a region in central Asia Minor, in modern Turkey. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that its name comes from Gaulish (Celtic) settlers who arrived about 280 BC, and that it became a Roman province in 25 BC. Paul passed through "the region of Galatia" with Phrygia on his second journey…

Iconium was a city in south-central Asia Minor, modern Konya in Turkey, where Paul and Barnabas preached on the first missionary journey. They came there after being driven out of Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:51). In the synagogue at Iconium, a great number of Jews and Greeks believed (Acts 14:1).…

Jarmuth was a Canaanite city in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah. Its king, Piram, joined Adonizedek of Jerusalem and the kings of Hebron, Lachish and Eglon in attacking Gibeon after it made peace with Israel. Joshua defeated the five kings, and they were later brought out of the cave…

Laodicea was a city of the Roman province of Asia in the Lycus valley, near Colossae and Hierapolis. Writing to the Colossians, Paul speaks of his concern for those at Laodicea who had not seen him in person (Col 2:1) and of Epaphras's zeal for them (Col 4:13). He greets the believers there, along…

Luz was the earlier name of the Canaanite city that became Bethel, in the hill country north of Jerusalem. Jacob named the place Bethel after his dream there, though the city was first called Luz (Gen 28:19). He later returned there with his household (Gen 35:6) and told Joseph that God Almighty…

Lystra was a city of Lycaonia in south-central Asia Minor, where Paul and Barnabas fled after being threatened at Iconium (Acts 14:6). There Paul healed a man who had been lame from birth (Acts 14:8). According to the wider chapter, the crowd took Barnabas and Paul for the gods Jupiter and Mercury…

Machpelah was a cave, together with the field around it, near Hebron in Canaan, described as lying "before Mamre" (Gen 23:17, 19). The name is usually taken to mean "double," and the Greek Septuagint calls it the "double cave" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Abraham bought the field…

Mamre was a place near Hebron in Canaan, closely tied to Abraham and his family. Genesis even equates it with Hebron, also called the city of Arbah (Gen 23:19; Gen 35:27). The cave of Machpelah, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite as a family burial place, lay in a field described as…

Mareshah was a city in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah. It is listed with Keilah and Achzib among the towns allotted to the tribe (Josh 15:44). Rehoboam later fortified it as one of his defensive cities (2 Chr 11:8). When Zerah the Ethiopian advanced with a vast army as far as Mareshah, King Asa…

Migdol, meaning “tower,” is the name of a place on Egypt’s eastern frontier. During the Exodus the Israelites camped before Pihahiroth, “between Migdol and the sea,” facing Baalzephon (Exod 14:2; Num 33:7). Jeremiah names a Migdol as one of the Egyptian towns where Jews lived after the fall of…

Millo was a fortification within ancient Jerusalem, closely linked with the City of David. It already existed when David took the city, since he built "from Millo and inward" (2 Sam 5:9; 1 Chr 11:8). Solomon raised forced labor to build it alongside the temple, his palace and the city wall, and his…

Mizpah was a place in Gilead, east of the Jordan, named when Laban and Jacob parted and set up a heap of stones as a witness between them, with Laban saying, "The LORD watch between me and thee" (Gen 31:49). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "watchtower." In the time of the judges the…

Netophah was a town in Judah, closely linked with Bethlehem. It is best known through the men called Netophathites. Two of David's mighty men came from there: Maharai and Heleb (or Heled) the son of Baanah (2 Sam 23:28–29; 1 Chr 11:30). Maharai, of the Zerahite clan, also commanded the division of…

Nob was a city of priests near Jerusalem in the time of Saul. David came there alone while fleeing Saul and was met by the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub (1 Sam 21:1). Doeg the Edomite saw this and reported it to Saul, who summoned Ahimelech and all the priests of Nob. Afterward the city was put to…

Philistia was the land of the Philistines, the coastal plain along the Mediterranean in southwest Canaan. The Hebrew name, Pelesheth, appears in the King James Version as "Philistia" in the Psalms and as "Palestina" in Exod 15:14 and Isa 14:29–31. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes it as a fertile…

Saron is the Greek form of Sharon used by the King James Version in Acts 9:35. It names the broad coastal plain between the central hill country and the Mediterranean, the district in which Lydda stood. After Peter healed the paralysed Aeneas at Lydda, the people living there and in Saron turned to…

Sepharvaim was a city whose people the king of Assyria resettled in the cities of Samaria after the Israelites were deported (2 Kgs 17:24). The Sepharvites burned their children in fire to their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech (2 Kgs 17:31). Sennacherib's officials later named it among the cities…

Shephelah is a Hebrew name meaning "lowland." It refers to the region of low, rolling hills between the Judean mountains to the east and the coastal plain to the west. The King James Version translates it variously as "vale," "low plains" and "low country." The sycamore-fig trees that grew there in…
